name: United Nations
governance_structure: Six principal organs: a General Assembly, a Security Council, an Economic and Social Council, a Trusteeship Council, an International Court of Justice and a Secretariat. The Security Council has fifteen members, five of them permanent; a substantive decision requires nine votes including the concurring votes of the permanent members.

name: North Atlantic Treaty Organization
governance_structure: Established by the North Atlantic Treaty (1949). Article 5 provides that an armed attack against one or more members shall be considered an attack against them all. Article 9 establishes a Council on which each member is represented, empowered to set up subsidiary bodies including a defence committee.

name: International Monetary Fund
governance_structure: Governed under its Articles of Agreement by a Board of Governors, an Executive Board and a Managing Director. Voting power is weighted by quota rather than one-member-one-vote: each member has basic votes plus one vote per part of its quota.

name: World Health Organization
governance_structure: Established by a Constitution that entered into force in 1948. The World Health Assembly, composed of delegates representing Members, is the supreme decision-making body, and an Executive Board gives effect to its decisions and policies.

name: World Trade Organization
governance_structure: Established by the Marrakesh Agreement (1994). A Ministerial Conference meeting at least once every two years is the top decision-making body, with a General Council between sessions. The WTO continues the GATT practice of decision-making by consensus.

name: European Commission
governance_structure: The executive of the European Union under the Treaty on European Union. The Commission promotes the general interest of the Union and shall be completely independent; its members are chosen on the ground of their general competence and European commitment.

name: International Labour Organization
governance_structure: Uniquely tripartite. The Constitution gives each member four representatives at the General Conference: two shall be government delegates and the other two represent employers and workpeople. Every delegate is entitled to vote individually, not as a national bloc.
